title: Minimum Cost to Connect Sticks
description: Brute force to optimized: re-sorting after every join versus a min-heap giving O(log n) access to the two shortest sticks, Huffman-style.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given the lengths of sticks, connect all of them into one stick. The cost of connecting two sticks is the sum of their lengths. Return the minimum total cost to connect all the sticks into one.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Every join's cost gets ADDED to every later join it participates in","Join the smallest sticks first, so their cost is \"carried forward\" the fewest times"],["Repeatedly need \"the two smallest values\" as the collection changes","A min-heap, giving O(log n) access to the current smallest values"]]}

blocks.text: Repeatedly join any two sticks into one (paying a cost equal to their combined length), until only one stick remains, choosing the joining order that minimizes the total cost paid across all joins.

blocks.title: Analogy: Merging Files With a Cost Proportional to Their Combined Size
blocks.text: Picture repeatedly merging pairs of files into one, where merging costs exactly the combined size of the two files being merged, and needing to choose a merge order that minimizes total cost, exactly like Huffman-style optimal merging.

blocks.caption: Always joining the two shortest sticks first minimizes their length being re-counted later

blocks.text: Joining 2 and 3 first (cost 5), then joining that with 4 (cost 9), gives a total cost of 14.
The optimal joining order gives a total cost of 30.

Before trying every possible joining order, notice that a stick's length gets added to the total cost once for every join it participates in afterward, so joining SHORT sticks first minimizes how many times their length gets "carried forward."

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Every join adds the combined length of the two sticks being joined to the total cost, and that combined stick may itself be joined again later, adding its length again.

Observation 2: To minimize the total, the sticks contributing to the MOST joins (deepest in the "merge tree") should be as SHORT as possible, exactly the same reasoning behind Huffman coding's optimal merge strategy.

Observation 3: Always joining the two currently shortest sticks greedily achieves this, since it keeps larger sticks out of early, frequently-recounted joins.

Observation 4: A min-heap gives O(log n) access to the two currently shortest sticks at every step, without needing to re-sort the whole collection each time.
This leads to a greedy strategy, always joining the two currently shortest sticks, implemented efficiently with a min-heap.
Sort the remaining sticks after every join, take the two shortest, join them, and repeat.

items: Sort the sticks in ascending order.
Remove the two shortest, add their sum to the total cost, and insert the combined length back.
Re-sort and repeat until one stick remains.

codes.python:
def connect_sticks(sticks):
    sticks = sorted(sticks)
    cost = 0
    while len(sticks) > 1:
        a, b = sticks[0], sticks[1]
        sticks = sticks[2:]
        combined = a + b
        cost += combined
        sticks.append(combined)
        sticks.sort()                          # re-sort from scratch every round
    return cost

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The array is fully re-sorted after every join to correctly find the next two shortest sticks.
This repeats the full sorting cost every round, even though only one new value is added each time.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared log n), up to n rounds, each with an O(n log n) sort.
Space: O(n).
Limitation: only one new combined stick is added each round, but the brute force re-sorts everything, when a min-heap would maintain order incrementally.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why full re-sorting is wasteful: only two sticks are removed and one added each round; the rest of the order is unaffected.

What tracks the two smallest efficiently: a min-heap, giving O(log n) pop and push instead of an O(n log n) full sort.

The core idea: build a min-heap once, then repeatedly pop the two smallest, add their sum to the cost, and push the sum back, each step O(log n).

Build a min-heap from all stick lengths. While more than one stick remains, pop the two smallest, add their sum to the running cost, and push that sum back onto the heap. Return the total cost once only one stick remains.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: min-heap, pop the 2 smallest, push their sum back

codes.python:
import heapq

def connect_sticks(sticks):
    heap = list(sticks)
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    cost = 0
    while len(heap) > 1:
        a = heapq.heappop(heap)
        b = heapq.heappop(heap)
        combined = a + b
        cost += combined
        heapq.heappush(heap, combined)      # O(log n), no full re-sort
    return cost

blocks.text: Always joining the two currently shortest sticks is the same greedy strategy that Huffman coding uses to minimize total weighted merge cost: it keeps the shortest sticks participating in the fewest "carried forward" additions, and the longest sticks joined last, contributing their length only once. A min-heap provides the current two smallest values in O(log n) at every step, without ever needing a full re-sort.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), building the heap once and performing O(n) pop/push operations, each O(log n).
Space: O(n) for the heap.

blocks.text: Minimum Cost to Connect Sticks is a direct application of the Huffman-coding-style greedy: always combine the two smallest values first, implemented efficiently with a min-heap instead of repeated full sorts.

blocks.text: If the interviewer says "how do you decide the join order", think: always join the two currently smallest sticks, the same greedy as Huffman coding.

blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n squared log n) time; the optimized min-heap approach runs in O(n log n) time. Both use O(n) space.

items: Pattern: a min-heap, always combining the two smallest values, the same greedy behind Huffman coding.
Core Idea: maintain stick lengths in a min-heap; pop the two smallest each round, add their sum to the cost, and push the sum back.
Time: O(n squared log n) for the brute force, O(n log n) for the optimized min-heap.
Most Important Observation: joining the shortest sticks first minimizes how many times their length gets re-added in later joins.
Interview Difficulty: a standard heap application, quick once the Huffman-style greedy is recognized.
